The Business of Fashion

Agenda-setting intelligence, analysis and advice for the global fashion community.

brut.title: Retailers suffer worst month in 25 years | Retail industry | The Guardian

webpage.text:
Retailers suffer worst month in 25 years | Retail industry

Britain's retailers have suffered their grimmest month in a quarter of a century as deep price cuts in the summer sales failed to entice wary consumers into the shops, the CBI said today.

The monthly snapshot of the high street from the employers' organisation found that 61% of businesses said activity was lower in July than a year earlier while only 25% said it was higher.

The CBI said the resulting balance of -36 points was the weakest since it began its distributive trades survey in 1983 and that retailers expected another dismal month in August.

Andy Clarke, chairman of the CBI distributive trades panel, and retail director of Asda, said: "It is turning out to be a very grim summer for many retailers. Pressure from higher fuel and food prices is prompting many people to rein in their spending, proving that value retailing has never been more important.

"The faltering housing market has really depressed sales of home furnishings and white goods this month and the high street is still struggling, but supermarkets are faring better.

"The retail sector will have to focus more than ever on providing good value to customers if they want to keep the sun shining this summer."

Faced with consumer belt-tightening, the shops and stores surveyed by the CBI had been expecting July to be a poor month for business, but the negative expectations balance of -32 was far worse than the -7 points anticipated. In a potential blow to the rest of the economy, retailers said that they were slashing orders with their suppliers.

The reluctance to spend displayed in today's report confirms poor recent trading reports from individual retailers such as Marks & Spencer and John Lewis. Only supermarkets and sellers of footwear and leather goods bucked the downward trend. The CBI said sales of big-ticket items were especially weak, with every respondent selling durable household goods and furniture and carpets reporting that sales were down on a year ago. Clothing retailers also suffered.

Howard Archer, economist with Global Insight, said: "The CBI's July distributive trades survey is a real shocker, pointing to consumer spending starting off the third quarter very much on the back foot. Indeed, evidence is mounting that consumers are now reining in their spending appreciably in the face of seriously squeezed purchasing power and other significant pressures."

POLL: How are you spending your Black Friday?

----------------------------------------

YORK, ENGLAND - NOVEMBER 25: Black Friday deals are advertised in a shop window in the centre of York on November 25, 2025 in York, England. This year's later Budget falls in the week of the Black Friday sales leaving retailers concerned at the disruption in the run up to Christmas. Many shoppers are being more cautious with their spending until after tomorrow's budget and shops are considering extending the Sales beyond the weekend. (Photo by Ian Forsyth/Getty Images)


A Brief History of Black Friday

Black Friday, now known as the unofficial start of the holiday shopping season, has roots that stretch back more than half a century. The term originated in the 1960s in Philadelphia, when police officers began using “Black Friday” to describe the heavy traffic and chaos caused by suburban shoppers flooding the city the day after Thanksgiving ahead of the Army–Navy football game. Retailers initially opposed the phrase due to its negative connotation.

Over time, the meaning shifted. By the 1980s, retailers began rebranding Black Friday as the day stores finally turned a profit for the year—moving from being "in the red" to "in the black." The positive spin caught on, and retailers leaned into the shopping frenzy by offering doorbuster deals and limited-time discounts to attract customers.

The rise of big-box stores in the 1990s and 2000s helped cement Black Friday as a major retail event. Crowds lined up at dawn—sometimes overnight—for deep discounts. In recent years, traditional in-person sales have evolved with online deals, often starting earlier in the week, leading to the broader concept of “Cyber Week.”

Today, Black Friday is one of the busiest shopping days in the United States, symbolizing both the kickoff to holiday spending and the evolution of American retail culture.

webpage.text:
15 tips and tricks to make the most of Boxing Day sales in Birmingham

How to get the best out of the Boxing Day sales in Birmingham - are you heading out to bag a bargain?

Our guide to ,Christmas shopping in Birmingham,

Are you heading to the Boxing Day sales in Birmingham?

For those who are keen to bag a bargain - if you didn't find enough on Black Friday or the endless sales craziness which has been going on ever since - there are plenty of discounts in the city.

Maybe you have had so much turkey and TV you just HAVE to get out and walking in a nearby nature reserve just doesn't cut it.

You need retail therapy and maybe a coffee or two.

So how do you cope with the Boxing Day sales and get the most out of it?

Here's our guide to enjoy the sales, bag a bargain and come home relatively happy. Oh, and don't forget those reusable bags!


1. Know the opening and closing times


It might be a good idea to get there early to beat the crowds (but then you will probably find people have turned up before you, eagerly queuing up outside Next from the early hours of the morning).

Apart from Next, most stores are opening at sensible times.

And if you plan to go later on, or just can't there until the afternoon or evening, you'll need to know the closing times so you don't turn up too late.


2. Work out where you're going to park


If you're coming into the city by car, it's important to know the best parking options.

It will take some of the stress out of driving if you know your destination, rather than battling with congestion and roadworks but not having any certainty about where you are aiming for.


3. Don't forget your bags!

Plastic bags aren't given out freely these days which gives even more reason to carry your own. So consider taking some sturdy bags with you if you're hitting the sales. Do you want to be stuffing a bargain faux fur gillet into a Tesco plastic bag which once held your spuds?

You may want to invest in some stylish tote bags - hopefully someone has been generous and given you one for Christmas. If not we found some pretty cool Brummie themed ones here.

And remember to put your receipts in your purse or wallet because you won't find them again if you shove them into the reusable bag.


4. Find somewhere for a sit-down and a cuppa


Christmas shopping can be exhausting at the best of times - and you'll need to have a sit-down and a drink at some point.


5. If you are bringing a baby, know the best places


6. Go off the beaten track and head to independent shops


You don't always have to go to the main high street stores to get your Christmas shopping.

They might have plenty of choice but going up and down escalators to several different floors can be time-consuming if you're in a rush. If you already know what you want, or want something a bit different, consider going to a smaller shop instead.

Birmingham has loads of independent stores so there are plenty of options.


7. Start the day with a big breakfast


Getting up early and having a big breakfast to fuel you for the festive shopping will get things off to a good start.

If you don't have time to have breakfast at home, then set off anyway and find some food in the city centre before you get going on the Christmas shopping.


8. Consider avoiding the city centre altogether


If the thought of braving roadworks and congestion to get into the city centre - and then paying for parking - just isn't appealing, there is another option.

You could go to a retail park where there is free parking and do your Christmas shopping there instead.

Luckily, there are several excellent out-of-town shopping parks in and around Birmingham with plenty of free parking.


9. Leave the car at home


Traffic congestion and potential parking headaches might put you off taking the car into Birmingham for shopping.

Public transport is a great alternative option for getting around, though you are tied to travel timetables for times of arrival and departure so you have less control over your day.

If choosing the train, Birmingham New Street is directly under the Grand Central mall and right in the city centre, while Resorts World, next to the NEC, is less than 10 minutes on foot from Birmingham International station.

Information is available from public transport provider Centro at website www.centro.org.uk


10. Check prices and availability beforehand


One good tip for a satisfying shopping trip is to go online at home and check stock availability - you might also be able to reserve what you want for collection from the store later.

While you are looking on the web, compare prices with those at other retailers as this will give you some haggling power so you don't end up paying too much.


11. Wear comfy shoes


It's probably a good idea to wear some sensible, comfy shoes if you are going to be traipsing around the city centre all day and getting more and more weighed down by shopping bags.

Tottering about in five-inch Christian Louboutin stiletto heels like those above will take its toll on your feet, legs and back. Comfort wins over style in the Christmas shopping battle.


12. Stick to your budget


Try not to get swept along in a sales frenzy.

Have a budget in mind, to stop you going 'off list' and getting enticed by all the sale signs, special offers and attractive displays.

Cross check items on your mobile phone before paying; if you could get them for less, be charming but cheeky and ask if the shop will match a price or throw in extras.


13. Don't get extended warranties


Don’t pay for extended warranties - you are protected by consumer rights that won’t leave you out of pocket if something goes wrong, and if you pay for items over £100 with a credit card you are further protected by Section 75 of the Consumer Credit Act.

Under Section 75, the credit card company is as responsible as the retailer for any breach of contract or misrepresentation. This law was put in place in the 1970s and means you are never in the position of paying off something you didn't receive or which wasn't as it should have been.

So if you're buying something costing more than £100, pay for some or all of it on a credit card to ensure you're protected.


14. Check refund policies


You have no legal right of returning goods if you just change your mind or they were the wrong size, rather than faulty. Many shops will still give refunds but check before you part with your cash to make sure.

If something is faulty, you are entitled to a full refund within 30 days under the Consumer Rights Act 2015. This applies even if the item is on sale or second-hand.

After that time period, it isn't quite as straightforward - if you return goods within six months, the shop has to prove they weren't faulty when you bought them. And you do have up to six years after the purchase to make a complaint. But after a long period, it gets harder to obtain a full refund and you may have to accept a partial refund or credit note.


15. Keep hold of your receipts


For the reasons discussed above in the point on refunds, it's vital to keep receipts from your shopping spree.

Put them in a box or folder rather than amassing them in your wallet or purse or just letting them float around on the kitchen counter or in a drawer. It's so easy for these little pieces of paper to become lost or mislaid.

You need to stay organised with this aspect of shopping, or getting a refund or exchange could be far more difficult.

Put them in a box or folder rather than amassing them in your wallet or purse or just letting them float around on the kitchen counter or in a drawer. It's so easy for these little pieces of paper to become lost or mislaid. You need to stay organised with this aspect of shopping, or getting a refund or exchange could be far more difficult.
